questions.question: What is a linked list and how does it differ from an array?
questions.title: Linked List vs Array | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **linked list** is a sequence of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next node. Unlike arrays, nodes are **not stored in contiguous memory**. This gives O(1) insertion at the head but O(n) access by position.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand memory layout differences and can reason about complexity tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying linked lists are always better than arrays — each has strengths depending on the access pattern
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Draw the node-pointer mental model and clearly state the tradeoff table: O(1) insert head vs O(n) random access

sections.title: Node-Pointer Structure vs Contiguous Memory
sections.content: A linked list node typically looks like: `class Node { int data; Node next; }`. Nodes can live anywhere in memory — each node points to the next. **No random access**: to reach node at position 5 you must traverse from the head. **O(1) insert at head**: just create a new node and set its `next` to the current head. Arrays offer O(1) random access but O(n) mid-insertion due to shifting.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Array: O(1) access, O(n) mid-insert, fixed size
- Linked list: O(n) access, O(1) insert at head, dynamic size
- No index-based access in linked list — must traverse from head
- Extra memory per node: the `next` pointer (8 bytes in 64-bit JVM)
- Singly linked: one `next` pointer; doubly linked: `next` and `prev`
- Java's LinkedList is a doubly linked list

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A linked list stores data in nodes, where each node holds the data and a reference to the next node. Unlike arrays, these nodes are not in contiguous memory, so you can't access them by index in O(1). To get to position five, you start from the head and traverse through five nodes — that's O(n). The advantage is that inserting at the head is O(1) — you just create a new node and point it to the current head. I'd use a linked list when I need frequent insertions at the front and don't need random access.

questions.question: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
questions.title: Detect Cycle in Linked List | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use Floyd's Cycle Detection (tortoise and hare algorithm).** Use two pointers: slow moves one step at a time, fast moves two steps. If there's a cycle, they will eventually meet. O(n) time, O(1) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Pointer manipulation skills and knowledge of a classic algorithm
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Suggesting a HashSet approach (valid but O(n) space) without knowing Floyd's O(1) space solution
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the algorithm — Floyd's Cycle Detection — and explain intuitively why fast catches slow in a cycle

sections.title: Floyd's Tortoise and Hare
sections.content: Initialize `slow = head` and `fast = head`. In each iteration: `slow = slow.next`, `fast = fast.next.next`. If `fast` or `fast.next` becomes null, there is no cycle — return false. If `slow == fast` at any point, a cycle exists — return true. **Why it works**: in a cycle, fast gains one step per iteration on slow; they must eventually occupy the same node.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- HashSet approach: O(n) time, O(n) space — store visited nodes
- Floyd's approach: O(n) time, O(1) space — preferred
- fast pointer moves 2 steps; slow moves 1 step
- Must check `fast != null && fast.next != null` before each step
- Extension: to find the cycle start node, reset one pointer to head after they meet, move both one step at a time — they meet at the cycle start

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd use Floyd's Cycle Detection algorithm — also called the tortoise and hare. I initialize two pointers, both at the head. The slow pointer moves one step at a time and the fast pointer moves two steps. If there's no cycle, the fast pointer reaches null first. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer will eventually catch up to the slow pointer because it gains one step per iteration. When they meet, there's a cycle. This is O(n) time and O(1) space, which is better than using a HashSet to track visited nodes.

questions.question: How do you reverse a singly linked list in Java?
questions.title: Reverse Linked List Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use three pointers: prev, current, next.** Iterate through the list, reversing each node's pointer: save `current.next`, set `current.next = prev`, advance prev and current. When current is null, prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.

interviewer_intent.testing: Pointer manipulation precision — this is a classic test of whether you can think through pointer reassignment without losing the list
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to save next before overwriting current.next, which loses the rest of the list
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through a 3-node example step by step — shows you can communicate algorithm execution clearly

sections.title: Three-Pointer Reversal
sections.content: Start with `prev = null`, `current = head`. Each iteration: (1) save `next = current.next` before you lose it, (2) reverse: `current.next = prev`, (3) advance: `prev = current`, `current = next`. When `current == null`, the loop ends and `prev` is the new head. **Critical step**: save `next` FIRST — if you set `current.next = prev` first, you lose access to the rest of the list.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Three pointers: prev (starts null), current (starts head), next (temp)
- Order matters: save next → reverse pointer → advance both
- After loop: prev = new head (current = null)
- Time: O(n), Space: O(1)
- Recursive reversal is also O(n) but O(n) space due to call stack
- Reversing sublists (e.g., reverse from position m to n) is a common variant

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I use three pointers: prev initialized to null, current initialized to head, and a temp next pointer. In each iteration, I first save current.next into next — this is critical because I'm about to overwrite it. Then I set current.next to prev, reversing that link. Then I advance prev to current and current to next. When current reaches null, prev is pointing to the new head. I always draw a small example with three nodes to verify my logic before coding because pointer mistakes are easy to make.

questions.question: How do you find the middle element of a linked list?
questions.title: Find Middle of Linked List | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Use the fast and slow pointer technique.** Slow moves one step, fast moves two steps. When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle. O(n) time, O(1) space — no need to count the length first.

interviewer_intent.testing: Two-pointer technique applied to linked lists, and whether you avoid the naive two-pass approach
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Counting the length first (two passes) — the fast/slow pointer does it in one pass
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that for even-length lists there are two middles and clarify which one your implementation returns

sections.title: Fast and Slow Pointer in One Pass
sections.content: Initialize both `slow = head` and `fast = head`. While `fast != null && fast.next != null`: move `slow = slow.next`, `fast = fast.next.next`. When the loop ends, `slow` is at the middle. For a list of length 5 (1→2→3→4→5), slow stops at 3. For a list of length 6 (1→2→3→4→5→6), slow stops at 4 (second middle) by default.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Naive approach: count length (pass 1), traverse to length/2 (pass 2) — two passes
- Fast/slow: one pass, O(n) time, O(1) space
- Even length: `fast != null` condition → second middle; `fast.next != null` → first middle
- This technique underlies cycle detection and finding the start of a cycle
- Used in merge sort on linked lists: find middle, split, merge

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The elegant one-pass solution is the fast and slow pointer technique. Both start at head. Slow moves one step at a time, fast moves two steps. When fast can't move anymore — it's null or its next is null — slow is exactly at the middle. This avoids counting the length in a first pass. I'd also clarify with the interviewer: for an even-length list there are two middle nodes, and the choice of termination condition determines which one we return.

questions.question: What is the difference between singly linked list and doubly linked list?
questions.title: Singly vs Doubly Linked List | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: A **singly linked list** has each node pointing only to the next node. A **doubly linked list** has each node pointing to both next and previous nodes. Doubly linked lists support O(1) deletion of a known node and backward traversal, at the cost of extra memory per node.

interviewer_intent.testing: Data structure knowledge and ability to reason about memory vs functionality tradeoffs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that Java's LinkedList class is a doubly linked list
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect to real Java: LinkedList is doubly linked; mention that Deque operations (addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast) are all O(1) because of prev/next pointers

sections.title: One Pointer vs Two Pointers Per Node
sections.content: **Singly linked list node**: `{ data, next }`. Can only traverse forward. **Doubly linked list node**: `{ data, next, prev }`. Can traverse both directions. The key operational advantage: to **delete a node** when you have a direct reference to it, a singly linked list requires O(n) to find its predecessor; a doubly linked list does it in **O(1)** using the `prev` pointer.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Singly: less memory (one pointer), forward traversal only
- Doubly: more memory (two pointers), bidirectional traversal
- Doubly: O(1) deletion of a node you have a reference to
- Java's LinkedList: doubly linked list implementing Deque
- addFirst/addLast/removeFirst/removeLast all O(1) in Java's LinkedList
- LRU cache implementation typically uses doubly linked list + HashMap

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A singly linked list node has data and a next pointer only — traversal is one-directional. A doubly linked list adds a prev pointer, enabling backward traversal and O(1) deletion of a node when you have a direct reference to it. The tradeoff is extra memory per node. In Java, the LinkedList class is a doubly linked list, which is why all its deque operations — adding or removing from either end — are O(1). A practical use case is an LRU cache, which commonly uses a doubly linked list combined with a HashMap.

questions.question: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
questions.title: Detect Cycle Linked List Floyd Algorithm
questions.direct_answer: Use Floyd's cycle detection algorithm: a slow pointer moves one step and a fast pointer moves two steps — if they ever meet, a cycle exists.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of the tortoise-and-hare algorithm — a very common linked list interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a HashSet to track visited nodes, which works but uses O(n) space
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Offer both approaches and explain why Floyd's is preferred: O(1) space

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most efficient approach is Floyd's cycle detection algorithm, also called the tortoise and hare. You use two pointers starting at the head. The slow pointer moves one node at a time. The fast pointer moves two nodes at a time. If a cycle exists, the fast pointer will eventually lap the slow pointer and they'll meet at the same node. If there's no cycle, the fast pointer will reach null.

The code in Java: initialize both to head, then loop while fast is not null and fast.next is not null. Inside the loop, slow = slow.next and fast = fast.next.next. If slow equals fast, return true. After the loop, return false.

Why does this work? In a cycle, the fast pointer reduces the gap between itself and the slow pointer by one each iteration. So if the cycle length is k, they'll meet within k iterations after both enter the cycle.

The alternative is using a HashSet: add each visited node to the set, and if you try to add a node that's already there, you've found a cycle. This is simpler to reason about but uses O(n) extra space.

Floyd's is preferred in interviews because it's O(1) space and O(n) time. The HashSet approach is O(n) for both. Mentioning both and explaining why Floyd's is the better choice shows good judgment.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Floyd's algorithm: slow moves +1, fast moves +2 — if they meet, cycle exists
O(n) time, O(1) space — preferred over HashSet approach
HashSet approach: O(n) space — simpler but less optimal
While loop condition: fast != null && fast.next != null to prevent NullPointerException

questions.question: How do you reverse a singly linked list iteratively?
questions.title: Reverse Linked List Iteratively Java
questions.direct_answer: Use three pointers — prev, current, and next — to reverse the direction of each pointer one node at a time in a single pass.

interviewer_intent.testing: Pointer manipulation fluency — a foundational linked list problem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Losing the reference to the next node before changing the pointer, causing the list to be cut
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Draw the pointer diagram mentally, narrate each step, and handle null head edge case

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Reversing a linked list iteratively uses three pointers. I initialize prev to null, current to head, and next to null. Then I loop while current is not null.

Inside the loop, the order of operations matters critically. First, save next as current.next — this is essential because I'm about to overwrite that pointer. Second, set current.next to prev — this reverses the arrow. Third, move prev to current. Fourth, move current to the saved next.

After the loop ends, current is null and prev points to what was the last node, which is now the new head. Return prev.

Let me trace through a small example: for the list 1 → 2 → 3 → null. Start: prev=null, current=1. Iteration 1: save next=2, point 1 back to null, prev becomes 1, current becomes 2. Iteration 2: save next=3, point 2 back to 1, prev becomes 2, current becomes 3. Iteration 3: save next=null, point 3 back to 2, prev becomes 3, current becomes null. Loop ends. Return prev (node 3). Now the list is 3 → 2 → 1 → null.

This is O(n) time and O(1) space since we only use three pointer variables regardless of list length. Edge cases: null input returns null; single-node list returns the same node unchanged.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Order in loop: save next, reverse pointer, advance prev, advance current
Return prev after loop — it's the new head
O(n) time, O(1) space — single pass, no extra data structures

questions.question: How do you find the middle element of a linked list in one pass?
questions.title: Find Middle Linked List One Pass
questions.direct_answer: Use the fast-slow pointer pattern: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps — when fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

interviewer_intent.testing: Fast-slow pointer pattern applied to a simple problem
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Counting nodes first then traversing again — that's two passes and not the elegant solution expected
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Handle even-length lists: fast.next == null vs fast == null determines which middle node you return

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The naive approach is to count nodes in one pass and then traverse to position n/2 in a second pass. But the interviewer usually wants a one-pass solution.

The elegant solution is the fast-slow pointer pattern. Initialize both slow and fast to head. Then loop: slow moves one step, fast moves two steps. When fast has no more moves — meaning fast is null or fast.next is null — slow is at the middle.

For an odd-length list like 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5: when fast is at 5 (fast.next is null), slow is at 3, the true middle.

For an even-length list like 1 → 2 → 3 → 4: there's a choice of which middle to return. If the loop condition is fast != null and fast.next != null, slow lands on node 2 — the first middle. If you want the second middle, you can advance slow one more step or adjust the condition.

This is why it's worth asking the interviewer what to return for an even-length list — showing that awareness is itself a good signal.

Time complexity is O(n) since both pointers traverse at most n steps total. Space is O(1) since we only use two pointer variables.

This same fast-slow approach is used to split a linked list for merge sort.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Fast-slow pointers: slow += 1, fast += 2 — when fast ends, slow is at middle
O(n) time, O(1) space — single pass
Even-length: clarify which middle to return (first or second)
Same pattern used to split a list for merge sort
